title: Impermanence
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: Zoketsu Norman Fischer reads an essay written for the Shambhala Sun on impermanence, beginning with the death scene in the Mahaparinibbana Sutta, where the Buddha's last words are "all conditioned things have the nature of vanishing." Norman tells of a dream in which an ailing mother-in-law, nearly ninety, and Norman squeeze past each other in a Paris cafe doorway and trade sides, then argues that vanishing happens right now rather than later. Dogen's line "impermanence itself is Buddha nature" leads Norman to approve both the weeping monks and the calm monks in the sutra, since every grief Norman has known has deepened love. The essay closes on the Buddha's message that everything vanishes and practice continues.

sentences.text: Well, you missed Tim's talk yesterday, which was great.
I got very enthusiastic about it.
I forgot how great the practice is.
But Tim reminded me, and I got up this morning and the rest of yesterday with a lot of enthusiasm to keep on practicing.
So maybe ten more years.
That was good for ten years.
It really was wonderful.
So if you didn't hear it, maybe it was recorded or ask him to give it again sometime.
It's very nice to be back in Bellingham.
And I guess I missed a trip, right?
In October you would have been.
Yeah, in October.
So when I came in, I realized, I mean, I forgot about it.
I didn't think, oh, in October I didn't think about it.
But now that I come in March, it is March, right?
It's March.
Now that I come in March, I can tell when I look at people, I was supposed to see them.
Like, what happened?
How come I didn't see them then?
You know, it's hard to explain.
It's almost like my whole body and mind is in a rhythm of seeing my friends at certain times.
And when I don't, I notice it.
So it's very nice to be here and see you.
And I know, though, that in my absence you had a very strong practice period.
And that's wonderful.
And the same in Vancouver, where I usually appear in January and I didn't this year.
And also there, all kinds of things are going on.
A new place is being established and so this is great.
This makes me feel really happy.
What makes me feel really sad is that we lost Karen Rosenstiel.
Did you chant for her and mention that?
Yeah.
Some of you will know Karen.
She, Karen, and I don't, I haven't found out yet.
I have to get a hold of Jack Duffy, who was her main teacher, and find out exactly what happened, because I didn't even know she was unwell.
We haven't seen her for a while because she was, for a while there, really practicing like a maniac.
You know, both coming here all the time and also practicing with Jack Duffy in Seattle.
So she was very busy, Dharma lady.
And at some point it's got to be too much.
And so she was, we hadn't seen her for a while.
She was only practicing with Jack.
But she always made a big impression.
She was a big person physically and in her personality and full of faith and energy for the Dharma.
She had many, many problems, you know, physical problems.
She was mostly blind and all kinds of things.
And she just had a passion for the Dharma that was truly prodigious and inspiring.
And so it was kind of shocking, you know, all of a sudden somebody, I guess Nancy, you forwarded an email to me from Jack, and I had no idea that she passed on.
So, so we'll miss her here, even though we haven't seen her for a while, you know.
It's sad that she has passed on and I hope that it was okay.
Well, I guess that's very apropos of the talk that I want to give today, which is about impermanence.
And so I'm going to, this talk is actually an article I wrote for the Shambhala Sun that hasn't yet appeared in the Shambhala Sun.
So, but they asked me to write it because I guess they're doing an issue on impermanence and they asked me if I would write an essay for it.
And it so happened that in our Dharma seminar in the Bay Area, we were studying the Mahaparinibbana Sutta, which is the story about the Buddha's last days and passing.
I begin my essay with a scene from that Sutta.
*The scene of the Buddha's passing, as told in the Pali Canon's Mahaparinibbana Sutta, is starkly beautiful.
Three months before, the Buddha had announced to the community that he had renounced the light force and that in three months time he would pass on.
And now the time has come and he's lying surrounded by his disciples.
So he says, before I go, do you have any questions?
Are there any last questions?
Any last doubts?
And through the silence of everyone there, in his own clairvoyance, you know, you could see into their hearts, he realizes that everybody there is well established in awakening.
There are no more doubts.
There are no more questions.
And he then says his final words to them and to us.
These are the Buddha's final recorded words.
Now, monks, I declare to you, all conditioned things have the nature of vanishing.
Keep on diligently with your practice.
Those are his last words.*

And then the Buddha journeys back and forth through the various meditation states, from the most shallow to the most deep, back down through to the most shallow, back up to around the middle of the depth.
And while this is going on, some of the other disciples think that the Buddha has passed on.
And somebody else says, no, no, he hasn't passed on.
He's just coursing in the meditation states.
He's still alive.
And then from one of the middle meditation states, he finally passes on into part of the manna.

And the monks, it says in the sutra, who are not yet fully awakened, tore their hair, raised their arms, threw themselves down, twisting and turning, and cried out in their extreme grief, too soon, too soon.
But the fully awakened monastics remained mindful and said, all compound things are impermanent.
What's the use of crying?
What did you expect?
So Buddhist practitioners throughout the ages have always understood impermanence as the cornerstone of the teachings and of the practice.
All that exists is impermanent.
Absolutely nothing lasts.
Therefore, everything you grasp or hold on to, you will lose.
And when we don't fully appreciate this profound but radically simple truth, we're going to suffer, as did the monks who descended into misery and despair at the Buddha's passing.
When we do understand this simple and profound truth fully, we can have real peace and understanding, as did the monks who remain fully mindful and calm.
As far as classical Buddhism is concerned, impermanence is the number one inescapable and essentially painful fact of life.
It is the singular existential problem that the whole edifice of Buddhist practice is meant to address.
To understand impermanence at the deepest possible level, because everybody understands it at superficial levels, nobody argues against impermanence.
It's impossible.
We all understand, but do we really understand?
When we really understand and merge fully with the truth of impermanence, that's the Buddhist path.
That's the culmination of the Buddhist path.
And this is what the Buddha says in his final words.
Impermanence is inescapable.
Everything is going to vanish.
Therefore, there is nothing more important than continuing the path with diligence.
All other options either deny or short shrift the problem.
You can't escape.
You better do something.
A little while ago, I had a dream that I remembered, and I'm still remembering now.
In this dream, it takes place in some kind of hazy underground cellar.
Now that I'm thinking of it, I think it was like a cafe that I was in one time in Paris.
That's where it was.
Kind of a little dark, go down some stairs.
And in this place, my mother-in-law is there.
She's coming from one direction, I'm coming from the other direction, going toward each other.
And we're both trying to squeeze through a sort of dim doorway in this cafe, coming from opposite directions.
Now, I'm not a small person.
My mother-in-law also is not a small person.
And it's kind of a small passageway.
So for a moment, as we're each going our own direction, we get stuck in the doorway.
And finally, we scoochie through.
She gets to her side, and I get to my side.
So now, I'm on the side she was on.
She's now on the side I was on.
And that's the dream.
Now, it's not that surprising that I would dream about my mother-in-law because literally every day, I'm thinking about my mother-in-law.
Because her situation is pretty rough.
She's getting close to ninety.
And she has an array of health problems.
She's pretty much all the time in pain.
All the time.
She can't walk anymore.
For some reason, she can't sleep at night.
She's up about every hour, all night long.
And she's got neuropathy in her hands.
So she can barely, she's losing the use of her hands.
She lives with her husband, my father-in-law, who's a few years older than she is.
And he's got advanced Alzheimer's disease.
He can't speak a coherent sentence.
And he doesn't know who he is or where he is.
And he is her constant companion.
And she takes care of him.
Now, they have other people helping, of course.
Now, despite this situation, I'm pretty sure that my mother-in-law affirms life one hundred percent as she always has.
As far as I know, she has never entertained the idea of death.
All she wants and hopes for is a good and pleasant life.
And since she does not have this right now, although I'm sure she hopes for it every day, she is a pretty miserable person, as anybody in that situation would be.
And every day we call her up, and every day we get reports how you got through another day.
Wow.
So that's why every day I'm literally thinking of my mother-in-law.
So that's her.
Now, I, on the other hand, although somebody just told me I didn't look so good.
As far as I know, as far as I know, I'm reasonably healthy.
But like now I'm wondering.
But as far as I know, I'm pretty healthy.
You know, I go to the doctor, and the doctor doesn't think there's anything wrong with me.
And I have no expectation of dying anytime soon, although those of you who know me know I'm constantly thinking I'll die tomorrow.
But really, I don't expect so.
So this is me.
But despite all this, ever since I was a little boy, I've always been thinking about death.
And, you know, when I think about my life, I realize that the reality of death has been probably the main motivator for everything I've ever done in my life.
Why else would I end up wearing robes and spending my entire life in meditation centers if I wasn't thinking about death and wondering about it?
And when you, you know, I do a lot of talking to people and writing and all that.
And when you kind of look at all the things that I write and talk about, what am I always talking about?
Constantly talking about absence, disappearing, vanishing, nothingness, death.
You know, what a dour guy.
And I would say that it really is the honest truth that not a single day goes by when I'm not thinking.
If not, you know, most of the day, part of the day, some of the day, the idea of death crosses my mind pretty much every day and many times a day, unlike my mother-in-law.
So this dream is very interesting to me because of this.
The question is, is my mother-in-law about to pass over through the threshold from life to death?
Although she's temporarily stuck in a crowded doorway, that's where she's going.
Seems like it.
But if that's the logic of the dream, then in the dream I must be already dead myself.
But that's where she's going.
And I'm stuck in the same doorway trying to pass over from death to life.
Of course, you're laughing because it is absurd.
Like, you know, that's ridiculous.
But then again, I've always felt that life and death is ridiculous.
It really doesn't make any sense the more you think about it.
And as I say, I've been thinking about this for a long time.
And the more I think about it and contemplate it and feel my way into it, the less sense it makes to me too.
And I sometimes even wonder whether life and death isn't just a conceptual framework that we confuse ourselves with.
To be sure, people in our lives do seem to disappear.
And that having generally been the case with others, it seems reasonable to assume that this will be the case with oneself at some point.
But what does it all mean?
And how do you account for the many anomalies that appear in this conceptual framework when you look for them?
Like the universal lore about ghosts and spirits that virtually every culture has, the evidence that you hear people giving for rebirth, reincarnation.
It's very telling that a lot of religions refer to death as eternal life.
And in the Mahaparinibbana Sutta, the Buddha doesn't die.
He enters a state called parinibbana, full extinction, which is by definition something other than death.
And in general Buddhism, death isn't actually death.
It's a staging area for more life.
So there are a lot of very respectable and less respectable reasons to wonder about this question of life and death.
In our sangha in the Bay Area, for some reason, we didn't sort of try to do this, but it turns out that we have a lot of people who are older.
There's a lot of people in our sangha in their seventies and even in their eighties.
And a lot more my age in their sixties.
So when younger people come around, they never come back.
Who would want to?
But the more ancient a person is, the more comfortable they feel in our group.
But because we have such an old group, we're constantly contemplating the ideas of death and impermanence.
It just seems to pop up in all the teachings we study somehow.
And we think about this, all conditioned things pass away.
Nothing will remain as it once was.
The body changes as you age.
There's a little bit less strength, a little bit less flexibility, a little bit less resilience.
And in response to this and to a lifetime's experience, the mind changes as well.
The way one thinks of, views and feels about life and the world is very different when you're older.
Even the same thoughts that you had when you were young or in midlife take on a different flavor when you have those same thoughts in older age.

The other day, one of my friends who's about my age, who had studied Zen when she was young with the great Korean Zen master Sangsanim, said to me, Sangsanim would always say to all of us young Dharma students, soon dead, soon dead.
And she said, and I understood what he was saying and I thought, yes, that's really true.
Very Zen.
And it was almost funny the way he said it.
He said, now when I think of it, it's a lot more personal to me and a lot more poignant.
Those same words and those same thoughts have a different flavor now.
All conditioned things have the nature of vanishing.
What is impermanence after all?
Now, even a young person knows that death is coming probably later.
So why worry about it now?
What's the point of worrying now?
It's coming later.

And even if you are a sort of semi lunatic like I was when I was young and thinking about this all the time, let's face it, it's sort of like a philosophical problem when you're young, more than personal problem.
And of course, as we're older, we do think, oh yes, how much longer can there be?
Death is coming.
And now we do take it personally.
But even then, do we actually know what we're talking about?
What are we really thinking about when we think that way?
So death may be the ultimate loss, the ultimate impermanence, but on a lesser, more everyday scale, impermanence and the loss it entails really comes down to one word, later.
In other words, something is here now, in a particular way, probably later, not.
I am something now.
I have something now in a particular way, probably later, not.
Today is today.
Later on, it'll be yesterday.
So impermanence means later.
And later is the safest possible timeframe there is.
You can ignore it, because it's later.
It's not now.
Later is always later.
It never seems to arrive.
And even if it does arrive, well, you know, it'll arrive later.
In other words, even though we all understand impermanence intellectually, for most of us, most of the time, actual impermanence is irrelevant.
But the truth is, impermanence is not later.
It's now.
*All conditioned things have the nature of vanishing.
Right now, they have that nature.
They don't have that nature later.
They have that nature right now.* And that's what the Heart Sutra is talking about.
Form is emptiness.
Emptiness is no other than form.
Or the Diamond Sutra talks about it.
Everything is like a dream, like a bubble, like a dewdrop, like a flash of lightning.
So it's not that something is going to vanish later; it's that right now, everything is in some way vanishing before our eyes, squeezing uncomfortably through the crowded doorway of now.
We actually don't know whether we're coming or going.
Impermanence may be a deeper thought than we realize.
When you think about this, impermanence is not only loss; basically, it's change.
And change can be wonderful and very refreshing.
But even when it's wonderful and refreshing, it's always both good and bad because even the refreshing change entails some loss, because nothing new ever appears unless something old ceases to be.
They say this on New Year's Eve: out with the old, in with the new.
New Year's Eve is happy and sad at the same time.
A new year is coming—fresh possibilities.
An old year is gone forever.
Happy and sad at the same time, just like in the Parinibbana Sutta, tears and equanimity at the same time.
In one of his great essays, Dogen writes, "Impermanence is itself Buddha nature."
This seems pretty different from the classical Buddhist notion of impermanence, which emphasizes the loss side of the loss, change, renewal equation.
For Dogen, impermanence is not a problem to be overcome with diligent effort on the path.
Impermanence is the path.
Practice is not the way to overcome or cope with impermanence; it is the way to fully embrace it and completely live it.
He says in this essay, if you want to understand Buddha nature, you should intimately observe cause and effect over time.
When the time is ripe, Buddha nature appears.
Dogen explains this teaching in his usual inside out way.
We love to read Dogen; he's sort of the founding teacher of our style of practice.
It's always surprising the things that he says.
He talks about this saying of his.

He interprets it, saying that practice is not so much a matter of changing or improving the conditions of your outer or your inner life, as much as it is a way of embracing and completely appreciating those conditions, especially the condition of impermanence and loss.
When you practice, he says, the time becomes ripe.
Usually, if you say the time becomes ripe, this implies already a later, right?
Things are not ripe now; they will be ripe later.
But Dogen says, "No, no, that's not what I mean.
Time is always ripe.
Ripe is the nature of time.
Rightness is time.
Buddha nature always manifests in time because time is always impermanence and that's why time is always ripe.
This moment is always a moment of fulfillment."
Of course this is true.
Of course time is impermanence, and impermanence is time because time is change, development, and loss.
Present time is ungraspable.
The moment it occurs, it already falls into the past.
As soon as I'm here, I'm gone.
If this were not so, how could the me of this moment ever get out of the way so that the me of the next moment can appear?
Which means that my being here is thanks to my not being here.
If I were not not here, I couldn't be here.
When you say these things, it's ridiculous.
It's paradoxical.
It sounds like a joke or a trick of language.
But in actual living, it really seems to be the case.
It must be so.
Every now and then, I hope that some of you are experiencing this because every now and then, when you practice meditation in a retreat for some days, the texture of the world feels different.
You feel the vanishing effect of time, and nothing appears unless it appears in time.
And whatever appears in time vanishes at once.
And that's what the Buddha said on his deathbed: "Time is existence, impermanence, change, loss, growth, development.
Time is the best and the worst at the same moment."
And Dogen calls this immense, uncanny, strange process Buddha nature life.
And then he says something really interesting.
He says Buddha nature is no other than all are because all are is Buddha nature.
It's a funny way of speaking.
So what does he mean by all are?
Are means existence, being, time, impermanence, change.
All are means existence, being, time, impermanence, change, is never alone, never isolated, is always all inclusive.
In other words, we're all always in this together.
That's the nature of time and of being, and it can't be any other way.
One of the wonderful things about my life is I get to talk to a lot of people about their spiritual process.
This is a rare thing.
I do this all the time, so I learn a lot.
The other day I was talking to someone, a very experienced practitioner.

She told me she was beginning to notice that the persistent feeling of dissatisfaction, something being a little off, a little wrong, that she had always felt all her life in relation to other people, in relation to the world, in relation to her inner life, her outer life.
She was beginning to realize that this sort of nagging feeling of dissatisfaction was probably not about other people.
It was probably not about the world in general.
It was probably not even about her inner or outer circumstances, but probably, she said, it's built into the nature of me.
It's like not something wrong; it's like I'm wrong inherently.
In other words, the dissatisfaction was not about circumstances; it was deeply ingrained.

Before realizing this, she assumed that the dissatisfaction must be a personal feeling on her part in some way, a feeling that she hoped through many years of diligent Zen practice she would be able to correct.
But now she thought, "No, it's much worse than that.
It's utterly and completely hopeless because the dissatisfaction was not something about her; it was her."
I was very impressed with this.
It's a hard thing to see.

I think this is exactly what the Buddha was talking about when he spoke of the basic shakiness of our sense of subjectivity in his very famous and almost entirely misunderstood doctrine of anatta or not-self or non-self.

Though we all need healthy egos in order to operate normally in the world, it may be that the essential grounding of ego is the false notion of permanence, a notion that we all unthinkingly subscribe to, even though deep in our hearts we all know better.
"I am me.
I have been me.
I will be me."
Of course I can change and I want to change.
I want to improve, but I'm always here.
I'm always me, and I literally have never known any other experience.

But this ignores the reality that all conditioned things have the nature of vanishing and are vanishing constantly as a fundamental condition of their existing in time, and the nature of time is vanishing.
Well, it's no wonder that we feel, as my friend felt, a constant, deeply felt, nagging sense of something is not quite right, something is wrong.
There's a kind of sense of disjunction that we might very well interpret as something sourcing from a chronic personal failing.
That is, once we get over blaming it on our relatives, our government, and the rest of the world, we sort of roll it back little by little by little until we finally get down to it's my fault.
No wonder we would feel that way when built into the nature of our subjectivity is this sort of basic contradiction, but all are is buddha nature.
This means that the self is not, as we have always imagined, an improvable permanent isolated entity that we and we alone are responsible for.
No, the self is actually impermanence itself, which is by its nature, never alone, never isolated, constantly flowing, and absolutely immense buddha nature itself.
Gauguin says impermanence itself is buddha nature, and then he says, quite astonishingly, permanence is the mind that discriminates the wholesomeness and the unwholesomeness of all things.
Impermanence itself is buddha nature, and permanence is the mind that discriminates the wholesomeness and unwholesomeness of all things.
Permanence?
We thought Gauguin was a Buddhist.
Where did he get permanence from?
How did permanence sneak its way into Gauguin's discourse?
So now I'm coming back to my dream, stuck in the doorway with my mother-in-law.
Which side is which and who is going where?

Impermanence and permanence may simply be balancing concepts, words that give rise to feelings and thoughts that support one another in helping us to grope towards some kind of understanding and misunderstanding of our lives.
What Gauguin means by permanence here is exactly practice.

Practice is what he says it is, what he says permanence is: that we have the wisdom and the commitment to know the difference between what we want to commit ourselves to in this lifetime and what we want to let go of in this lifetime.
The mind that commits itself to that process is permanent, he says.
So the good news about impermanence is buddha nature is that we can finally let go.
We can finally let ourselves off the hook.
We can get rid of all of this pain.
We can let go of the great and endless chore of improving ourselves.

We can let go of the endless rat race of being stellar accomplished people inwardly and outwardly, and this is no small thing because we are all subject to this kind of brutal, almost violent inner pressure to be and do more today than we were and did yesterday and to be and do more than someone else has been and done today and will be and do tomorrow.
This subtle pressure is in all of us, and it really is brutal, and now we can really let it go.
That's the good news.
The bad news is this is immense.
How do we get a handle on this?
How do we how can we do anything about it?
How do we I mean what are we going to do?
Just repeat the words over and over again, and what do we do about it?
Because we still have our lives to live, and if we're not practicing for the ultimate great awakening and the ultimate perfect ability of ourselves, what are we doing and how do we do it?
Dogen answers this question for us.

If impermanence is the corrosive worm at the heart of the apple of self that makes suffering a built-in factor of human life, even with all the privilege and advantages that we have, we're suffering because of this.
If impermanence is that worm at the heart of our suffering, then impermanence is the beautiful flower, the petal that emerges from the sepal of the flower of impermanence.

It's this petal, this flower petal that makes happiness and even joy real, joy possible in our human life because the one thing that is absolutely reliable, the one thing that is really permanent, is impermanence.
This ongoing process of living and dying and time.
Permanence is nirvana, bliss, cessation, relief, the never-ending, ever-changing and growing field of practice.
People come and go—buildings, flowers, trees, skies—practice goes on and on.

In the Buddha's final scene as told in the Maha Parinibbana Sutta, the contrast between the monastics who tear their hair and raise their arms and throw themselves down in their extreme grief and the monastics who receive the Buddha's passing with equanimity, the contrast between them couldn't be greater.
We read the text, and the Sutta seems to be implying disapproval of the former and approval of the latter, but maybe not.
Maybe the approval and disapproval is actually in our reading and not in the text.
When I thought that I went back and looked at the text, I thought, "You know what?
It doesn't really—it's not.

You automatically assume that, but you don't have to assume that because if impermanence is permanence is Buddha nature, then loss really is loss, but it's also happiness and affirmation, and we can approve both sets of monks.
Maybe the Sutra means to tell us that it takes both.

Impermanence is not something that we're supposed to be overcoming and conquering; it's something that we're supposed to be living and appreciating because it reflects the all our side of our human nature.

The weeping and the wailing monastics, maybe we're expressing their confusion and attachment, but maybe they were also expressing or maybe the confusion and attachment itself was an expression of their full immersion in human life and of their love for someone that they revered.
One of the great blessings and curses of reaching an older age is that you experience this more and more, and I've experienced this more than once in times of great loss.

I usually don't tear my hair—well, there's not much there to be torn—and I usually don't throw myself on the ground and wave my arms around, but I have more than once felt extreme sadness and loss, and it seemed to me in those moments as if it wasn't just me but the entire world was weeping and had gone dark with the fresh absence of someone that I love.

So I know the feeling of those monastics tearing their hair and weeping and wailing, and at the same time in the same moment I felt some appreciation and equanimity and tremendous peace because loss, as searing as it can be, it's so truthful and so beautiful—sad, yes, and beautiful.
And my own tears and my own sadness and anguish are beautiful because they are the consequence of love.
And this has happened to me every time.
Each fresh grief makes me love the world and other people in all of life more and more, love with more and more grief.
Every single loss I've experienced, every personal and emotional teaching of impermanence that life has been kind enough to offer me has deepened my ability to love.
I think that people misunderstand the promise that practice offers us.
Practice is not promising us bliss, joy, transcendence all the time.
It's not promising us even the absence of difficulty.
Who would want that in a world in which there's so much injustice, so much tragedy, so much unhappiness, illness and death?

Who wants to feel light-hearted and happy and without trouble in a world like that to feel the scourge of impermanence and loss and to appreciate it at the same time profoundly as the beautiful essence of what it means to be at all?
This is the deep truth that I hear echoing in Buddha's last words: everything vanishes, practice continues.
So we all have to ask ourselves what's important, where do I stake my life?
And whether we put that question to ourselves, you know, in that stark way, dramatic way or not, if you're a human being, the question is there, and it will be answered.
It will be answered by your life.
Your life is the answer to that question.
So I'm so grateful to be able to live my life in the company of so many of you who are answering that question with courage and real strength, knowing what is important and acting on that.
And when you feel that and when you have confidence in that, then you can come when it's time to come and you can go when it's time to go.
It's beautiful.
It's okay.
So thanks to the community here for I always think, you know, I mean, yes, I suffered terribly waiting in the airport for my delayed flight.
Always me was just awful.

Meanwhile, everybody here is like working and madly to put on this retreat, cooking the food and shopping this that, and the other thing, I don't even know all that goes on to make this happen—the registrar, the people packing all their Zafus into their cars to get there and blah blah all this stuff.
And I sort of waltz in nice calm.
He's very calm.
No wonder I'm calm.
I don't have to do anything, so I'm well aware of all it takes to make this happen, all it takes to bring this hall into our lives and as a gathering place for everybody.
And the new place in Vancouver, anxious to see when I'm up there in May, this is a real offering to the world.
Thank you for doing it.
Thank you Tim and everybody in the community.
Take care.

verbatim.text: Well, so you missed Tim's talk yesterday, which was great. I got very enthusiastic about it. I forgot how great the practice is. But Tim reminded me, and I got up this morning and the rest of yesterday with a lot of enthusiasm to keep on practicing. So maybe ten more years. That was good for ten years. It really was wonderful. So if you didn't hear it, maybe it was recorded or ask him to give it again sometime. It's very nice to be back in Bellingham. And I guess I missed a trip, right? In October you would have been. Yeah, in October. So when I came in, I realized, I mean, I forgot about it. I didn't think, oh, in October I didn't think about it.

But now that I come in March, it is March, right? It's March. Now that I come in March, I can tell when I look at people, I was supposed to see them. Like, what happened? How come I didn't see them then? You know, it's hard to explain. It's almost like my whole body and mind is in a rhythm of seeing my friends at certain times. And when I don't, I notice it. So it's very nice to be here and see you. And I know, though, that in my absence you had a very strong practice period. And that's wonderful. And the same in Vancouver, where I usually appear in January and I didn't this year. And also there, all kinds

of things are going on. A new place is being established and so this is great. This makes me feel really happy. What makes me feel really sad is that we lost Karen Rosenstiel. Did you chant for her and mention that? Yeah. Some of you will know Karen. She, Karen, and I don't, I haven't found out yet. I have to get a hold of Jack Duffy, who was her main teacher, and find out exactly what happened, because I didn't even know she was unwell. We haven't seen her for a while because she was, for a while there, really practicing like a maniac. You know, both coming here all the time and also practicing with Jack

Duffy in Seattle. So she was very busy, Dharma lady. And at some point it's got to be too much. And so she was, we hadn't seen her for a while. She was only practicing with Jack. But she always made a big impression. She was a big person physically and in her personality and full of faith and energy for the Dharma. She had many, many problems, you know, physical problems. She was mostly blind and all kinds of things. And she just had a passion for the Dharma that was truly prodigious and inspiring. And so it was kind of shocking, you know, all of a sudden somebody, I guess Nancy, you forwarded

an email to me from Jack, and I had no idea that she passed on. So, so we'll miss her here, even though we haven't seen her for a while, you know. It's sad that she has passed on and I hope that it was okay. Well, I guess that's very apropos of the talk that I want to give today, which is about impermanence. And so I'm going to, this talk is actually an article I wrote for the Shambhala Sun that hasn't yet appeared in the Shambhala Sun. So, but they asked me to write it because I guess they're doing an issue on impermanence and they asked me if I would write an essay for it. And it

so happened that in our Dharma seminar in the Bay Area, we were studying the Mahaparinibbana Sutta, which is the story about the Buddha's last days and passing. So I begin my essay with a scene from that Sutta. The scene of the Buddha's passing, as told in the Pali Canon's Mahaparinibbana Sutta, is starkly beautiful. Three months before, the Buddha had announced to the community that he had renounced the light force and that in three months time he would pass on. And now the time has come and he's lying surrounded by his disciples. So he says, before I go, do you have any questions? Are

there any last questions? Any last doubts? And through the silence of everyone there, in his own clairvoyance, you know, you could see into their hearts, he realizes that everybody there is well established in awakening. There are no more doubts. There are no more questions. And he then says his final words to them and to us. These are the Buddha's final recorded words. Now, monks, I declare to you, all conditioned things have the nature of vanishing. Keep on diligently with your practice. Those are his last words. And then the Buddha journeys back and forth through the

various meditation states, from the most shallow to the most deep, back down through to the most shallow, back up to around the middle of the depth. And while this is going on, some of the other disciples think that the Buddha has passed on. And somebody else says, no, no, he hasn't passed on. He's just coursing in the meditation states. He's still alive. And then from one of the middle meditation states, he finally passes on into part of the manna. And the monks, it says in the sutra, who are not yet fully awakened, tore their hair, raised their

arms, threw themselves down, twisting and turning, and cried out in their extreme grief, too soon, too soon. But the fully awakened monastics remained mindful and said, all compound things are impermanent. What's the use of crying? What did you expect? So Buddhist practitioners throughout the ages have always understood impermanence as the cornerstone of the teachings and of the practice. All that exists is impermanent. Absolutely nothing lasts. Therefore, everything you grasp or hold on to, you will

lose. And when we don't fully appreciate this profound but radically simple truth, we're going to suffer, as did the monks who descended into misery and despair at the Buddha's passing. When we do understand this simple and profound truth fully, we can have real peace and understanding, as did the monks who remain fully mindful and calm. As far as classical Buddhism is concerned, impermanence is the number one inescapable and essentially painful fact of life. It is the singular existential

problem that the whole edifice of Buddhist practice is meant to address. To understand impermanence at the deepest possible level, because everybody understands it at superficial levels, nobody argues against impermanence. It's impossible. We all understand, but do we really understand? When we really understand and merge fully with the truth of impermanence, that's the Buddhist path. That's the culmination of the Buddhist path. And this is what the Buddha

says in his final words. Impermanence is inescapable. Everything is going to vanish. Therefore, there is nothing more important than continuing the path with diligence. All other options either deny or short shrift the problem. You can't escape. You better do something. A little while ago, I had a dream that I remembered, and I'm still remembering now. In this dream, it takes place in some kind of hazy underground cellar. Now that I'm thinking of it, I think it

was like a cafe that I was in one time in Paris. That's where it was. Kind of a little dark, go down some stairs. And in this place, my mother-in-law is there. She's coming from one direction, I'm coming from the other direction, going toward each other. And we're both trying to squeeze through a sort of dim doorway in this cafe, coming from opposite directions. Now, I'm not a small person. My mother-in-law also is not a small person.

And it's kind of a small passageway. So for a moment, as we're each going our own direction, we get stuck in the doorway. And finally, we scoochie through. She gets to her side, and I get to my side. So now, I'm on the side she was on. She's now on the side I was on. And that's the dream. Now, it's not that surprising that I would dream about my mother-in-law because literally every day, I'm thinking about my mother-in-law. Because

her situation is pretty rough. She's getting close to 90. And she has an array of health problems. She's pretty much all the time in pain. All the time. She can't walk anymore. For some reason, she can't sleep at night. She's up about every hour, all night long. And she's got neuropathy in her hands. So she can barely, she's losing the use of her hands. She lives with her husband, my father-in-law, who's a

few years older than she is. And he's got advanced Alzheimer's disease. He can't speak a coherent sentence. And he doesn't know who he is or where he is. And he is her constant companion. And she takes care of him. Now, they have other people helping, of course. Now, despite this situation, I'm pretty sure that my mother-in-law affirms life 100 percent as she always has. As far as I know, she

has never entertained the idea of death. All she wants and hopes for is a good and pleasant life. And since she does not have this right now, although I'm sure she hopes for it every day, she is a pretty miserable person, as anybody in that situation would be. And every day we call her up, and every day we get reports how you got through another day. Wow. So that's why every

day I'm literally thinking of my mother-in-law. So that's her. Now, I, on the other hand, although somebody just told me I didn't look so good. As far as I know, as far as I know, I'm reasonably healthy. But like now I'm wondering. But as far as I know, I'm pretty healthy. You know, I go to the doctor, and the doctor doesn't think there's anything wrong with me.

And I have no expectation of dying anytime soon, although those of you who know me know I'm constantly thinking I'll die tomorrow. But really, I don't expect so. So this is me. But despite all this, ever since I was a little boy, I've always been thinking about death. And, you know, when I think about my life, I realize that the reality of death has been

probably the main motivator for everything I've ever done in my life. Why else would I end up wearing robes and spending my entire life in meditation centers if I wasn't thinking about death and wondering about it? And when you, you know, I do a lot of talking to people and writing and all that. And when you kind of look at all the things

that I write and talk about, what am I always talking about? Constantly talking about absence, disappearing, vanishing, nothingness, death. You know, what a dour guy. And I would say that it really is the honest truth that not a single day goes by when I'm not thinking. If not, you know, most of the day, part of the

day, some of the day, the idea of death crosses my mind pretty much every day and many times a day, unlike my mother-in-law. So this dream is very interesting to me because of this. The question is, is my mother-in-law about to pass over through the threshold from life to death? Although she's temporarily stuck in a crowded

doorway, that's where she's going. Seems like it. But if that's the logic of the dream, then in the dream I must be already dead myself. But that's where she's going. And I'm stuck in the same doorway trying to pass over from death to life. Of course, you're laughing because it is absurd. Like, you

know, that's ridiculous. But then again, I've always felt that life and death is ridiculous. It really doesn't make any sense the more you think about it. And as I say, I've been thinking about this for a long time. And the more I think about it and contemplate it and feel my way into it, the less

sense it makes to me too. And I sometimes even wonder whether life and death isn't just a conceptual framework that we confuse ourselves with. To be sure, people in our lives do seem to disappear. And that having generally been the case with others, it seems reasonable to assume that

this will be the case with oneself at some point. But what does it all mean? And how do you account for the many anomalies that appear in this conceptual framework when you look for them? Like the universal lore about ghosts and spirits that virtually every culture has, the evidence that you

hear people giving for rebirth, reincarnation. It's very telling that a lot of religions refer to death as eternal life. And in the Mahaparinibbana Sutta, the Buddha doesn't die. He enters a state called parinibbana, full extinction, which is by definition something other than death.

And in general Buddhism, death isn't actually death. It's a staging area for more life. So there are a lot of very respectable and less respectable reasons to wonder about this question of life and death. In our sangha in the Bay Area, for some reason, we didn't sort of try to do this, but

it turns out that we have a lot of people who are older. There's a lot of people in our sangha in their 70s and even in their 80s. And a lot more my age in their 60s. So when younger people come around, they never come back. Who would want to? But the more ancient a person is, the more

comfortable they feel in our group. But because we have such an old group, we're constantly contemplating the ideas of death and impermanence. It just seems to pop up in all the teachings we study somehow. And we think about this, all conditioned things pass away. Nothing will remain

as it once was. The body changes as you age. There's a little bit less strength, a little bit less flexibility, a little bit less resilience. And in response to this and to a lifetime's experience, the mind changes as well. The way one thinks of, views and feels about

life and the world is very different when you're older. Even the same thoughts that you had when you were young or in midlife take on a different flavor when you have those same thoughts in older age. The other day, one of my friends who's about my age, who had studied

Zen when she was young with the great Korean Zen master Sangsanim, said to me, Sangsanim would always say to all of us young Dharma students, soon dead, soon dead. And she said, and I understood what he was saying and I thought, yes, that's really true. Very Zen. And it was

almost funny the way he said it. He said, now when I think of it, it's a lot more personal to me and a lot more poignant. Those same words and those same thoughts have a different flavor now. All conditioned things have the nature of vanishing. What is impermanence after all? Now, even

a young person knows that death is coming probably later. So why worry about it now? What's the point of worrying now? It's coming later. And even if you are a sort of semi lunatic like I was when I was young and thinking about this all the time, let's face it, it's sort of like a

philosophical problem when you're young, more than personal problem. And of course, as we're older, we do think, oh yes, how much longer can there be? Death is coming. And now we do take it personally. But even then, do we actually know what we're talking about? What are we really

thinking about when we think that way? So death may be the ultimate loss, the ultimate impermanence, but on a lesser, more everyday scale, impermanence and the loss it entails really comes down to one word, later. In other words, something is here now, in a particular way,

probably later, not. I am something now. I have something now in a particular way, probably later, not. Today is today. Later on, it'll be yesterday. So impermanence means later. And later is the safest possible timeframe there is. You can ignore it, because it's later. It's

not now. Later is always later. It never seems to arrive. And even if it does arrive, well, you know, it'll arrive later. In other words, even though we all understand impermanence intellectually, for most of us, most of the time, actual impermanence is irrelevant. But the

truth is, impermanence is not later. It's now. All conditioned things have the nature of vanishing. Right now, they have that nature. They don't have that nature later. They have that nature right now. And that's what the Heart Sutra is talking about. Form is emptiness. And

emptiness is no other than form. Or the Diamond Sutra talks about it. Everything is like a dream, like a bubble, like a dewdrop, like a flash of lightning. So it's not that something is going to vanish later. It's that right now, everything is in some way. And though we don't

understand in what way, vanishing before our eyes, squeezing uncomfortably through the crowded doorway of now, we actually don't know whether we're coming or going. Impermanence may be a deeper thought than we realize. Now, when you think about this, impermanence is

not only loss. Basically, it's change. And change can be wonderful and very refreshing. But even when it's wonderful and refreshing, it's always both good and bad because even the refreshing change entails some loss. Because nothing new ever appears unless something old ceases

to be. They say this on New Year's Eve, you know, out with the old, in with the new. New Year's Eve is happy and sad at the same time. A new year is coming. Fresh possibilities. An old year is gone forever. Happy and sad at the same time. Just like in the Parinibbana

Sutta, tears and equanimity at the same time. In one of his great essays, Dogen writes, impermanence is itself Buddha nature. Impermanence is itself Buddha nature. This seems pretty different from the classical Buddhist notion of impermanence, which emphasizes the loss side of the loss,

change, renewal equation. For Dogen, impermanence is not a problem to be overcome with diligent effort on the path. Impermanence is the path. Practice is not the way to overcome or cope with impermanence. It is the way to fully embrace it and completely live it. He says in this

essay, if you want to understand Buddha nature, you should intimately observe cause and effect over time. When the time is ripe, Buddha nature appears. Dogen explains this teaching in his usual inside out way. We love to read Dogen. He's sort of the founding teacher of our style of practice. It's

always surprising the things that he says. He talks about this saying of his. He interprets it. He says that practice is not so much a matter of changing or improving the conditions of your outer or your inner life, as much as it is a way of embracing and completely appreciating those

conditions, especially the condition of impermanence and loss. When you practice, he says, the time becomes ripe. Usually if you say the time becomes ripe, this implies already a later, right? Things are not ripe now. They will be ripe later. But Dogen says, no, no, that's not what I mean.

Time is always ripe. Ripe is the nature of time. Rightness is time. Buddha nature always manifests in time because time is always impermanence and that's why time is always ripe. This moment is always a moment of fulfillment. Of course this is true. Of course time is impermanence and impermanence is time

because time is change, development, and loss. Present time is ungraspable. The moment it occurs, it already falls into the past. As soon as I'm here, I'm gone. If this were not so, how could the me of this moment ever get out of the way so that the me of the next moment can appear? Which means that my

being here is thanks to my not being here. If I were not not here, I couldn't be here. When you say these things, it's ridiculous. It's paradoxical. It sounds like a joke or a trick of language. But in actual living, it really seems to be the case. It must be so. Every now and then, I hope

that some of you are experiencing this because every now and then, when you practice meditation in a retreat for some days, the texture of the world feels different. You feel the vanishing effect of time and nothing appears unless it appears in time. And whatever appears in time vanishes at once.

And that's what the Buddha said on his deathbed. Time is existence, impermanence, change, loss, growth, development. Time is the best and the worst at the same moment. And Dogen calls this immense, uncanny, strange process Buddha nature life. And then he says something really interesting. He

says Buddha nature is no other than all are because all are is Buddha nature. It's a funny way of speaking. So what does he mean by all Buddha nature is all are? Are means existence, being, time, impermanence, change. All are means existence, being, time, impermanence, change, is never alone,

never isolated, is always all inclusive. In other words, we're all always in this together. That's the nature of time and of being and it can't be any other way. One of the wonderful things about my life is I get to talk to a lot of people about their spiritual process. This is a rare thing. I do

this all the time. So I learn a lot. The other day I was talking to someone, a very experienced practitioner. She told me she was beginning to notice that the persistent feeling of dissatisfaction, something you know being a little off, a little wrong, that she had always

felt all her life in relation to other people, in relation to the world, in relation to her inner life, her outer life. She was beginning to realize that this sort of nagging feeling of dissatisfaction was probably not about other people. It was probably not about the world in general.

It was probably not even about her inner or outer circumstances, but probably, she said, it's built into the nature of me. It's like not something wrong. It's like I'm wrong inherently. In other words, the dissatisfaction was not about circumstances. It was deeply ingrained. Before realizing this, she

said, she assumed that the dissatisfaction must be a personal feeling on her part in some way, a feeling that she hoped through many years of diligent Zen practice she would be able to correct, but now she thought, no, it's much worse than that. It's utterly and completely

hopeless because the dissatisfaction was not something about her. It was her. I was very impressed with this. It's a hard thing to see. I think this is exactly what the Buddha was talking about when he spoke of the basic shakiness of our sense of subjectivity in his very famous and

almost entirely misunderstood doctrine of anatta or not-self or non-self, though we all need healthy egos in order to operate normally in the world. It may be that the essential grounding of ego is the false notion of permanence, a notion that we all unthinkingly subscribe to, even though

deep in our hearts we all know better. I am me. I have been me. I will be me. Of course I can change and I want to change. I want to improve, but I'm always here. I'm always me and I literally have never known any other experience, but this ignores the reality that all conditioned things

have the nature of vanishing and are vanishing constantly as a fundamental condition of their existing in time and the nature of time is vanishing. Well, it's no wonder that we feel, as my friend felt, a constant, deeply felt, nagging sense of something is not quite right, something is wrong. There's a

kind of sense of disjunction that we might very well interpret as something sourcing from a chronic personal failing. That is, once we get over blaming it on our relatives, our government, and the rest of the world, we sort of roll it back little by little by little until we finally get

down to it's my fault. No wonder we would feel that way when built into the nature of our subjectivity is this sort of basic contradiction, but all are is buddha nature. This means that the self is not, as we have always imagined, an improvable permanent isolated entity that we and we alone

are responsible for. No, the self is actually impermanence itself, which is by its nature, never alone, never isolated, constantly flowing, and absolutely immense buddha nature itself. Gauguin says impermanence itself is buddha nature, and then he says, quite astonishingly, permanence is the mind

that discriminates the wholesomeness and the unwholesomeness of all things. Impermanence itself is buddha nature, and permanence is the mind that discriminates the wholesomeness and unwholesomeness of all things. Permanence? We thought Gauguin was a Buddhist. Where did

he get permanence from? How did permanence sneak its way into Gauguin's discourse? So now I'm coming back to my dream, stuck in the doorway with my mother-in-law. Which side is which and who is going where? Impermanence and permanence may simply be balancing concepts, words that give rise to

feelings and thoughts that support one another in helping us to grope towards some kind of understanding and misunderstanding of our lives. What Gauguin means by permanence here is exactly practice. Practice is what he says it is, what he says permanence is. That we have the wisdom and the

commitment to know the difference between what we want to commit ourselves to in this lifetime and what we want to let go of in this lifetime. The mind that commits itself to that process is permanent, he says. So the good news about impermanence is buddha nature is that we can finally let go.

We can finally let ourselves off the hook. We can get rid of all of this pain. We can let go of the great and endless chore of improving ourselves. We can let go of the endless rat race of being stellar accomplished people inwardly and outwardly and this is no small thing because we are all subject

to this kind of brutal almost violent inner pressure to be and do more today than we were and did yesterday and to be and do more than someone else has been and done today and will be and do tomorrow. This subtle pressure is in all of us and it really is brutal and now we can really let it go. That's the

good news. The bad news is this is immense. How do we get a handle on this? How do we how can we do anything about it? How do we I mean what are we going to do? Just repeat the words over and over again and what do we do about it? Because we still have our lives to live and if we're not

practicing for the ultimate great awakening and the ultimate perfect ability of ourselves what are we doing and how do we do it? Dogen answers this question for us. If impermanence is the corrosive worm at the heart of the apple of self that makes suffering a built-in factor of

human life even with all the privilege and you know advantages that we have we're suffering because of this. If impermanence is that worm at the heart of our suffering then impermanence is the beautiful flower the petal that emerges from the sepal of the flower of impermanence. It's this

petal this flower petal that makes happiness and even joy real joy possible in our human life because the one thing that is absolutely reliable the one thing that is really permanent is impermanence. This ongoing process of living and dying and time. Permanence is nirvana, bliss

cessation, relief, the never-ending ever-changing and growing field of practice. People come and go. Buildings flowers, trees, skies, practice goes on and on. In the Buddha's final scene as told in the Maha Parinibbana Sutta the contrast between the monastics who tear their hair and raise their arms

and throw themselves down in their extreme grief and the monastics who receive the Buddha's passing with equanimity the contrast between them couldn't be greater. We read the text and the Sutta seems to be implying disapproval of the former and approval of the latter but maybe not. Maybe the

approval and disapproval is actually in our reading and not in the text and when I thought that I went back and looked at the text and I thought you know what it doesn't really it's not you automatically assume that but you don't have to assume that because if impermanence is permanence is

Buddha nature then loss really is loss but it's also happiness and affirmation and we can approve both sets of monks maybe the Sutra means to tell us that it takes both. Impermanence is not something that we're supposed to be overcoming and conquering it's something that we're supposed to be

living and appreciating because it reflects the all our side of our human nature. The weeping and the wailing monastics maybe we're expressing their confusion and attachment but maybe they were also expressing or maybe the confusion and attachment itself was an expression of their full immersion in

human life and of their love for someone that they revered and one of the great blessings and curses of reaching an older age is that you experience this more and more and I've experienced this more than once in times of great loss. I usually don't tear my hair well there's not much

there to be torn and I usually don't throw myself on the ground and wave my arms around but I have more than once felt extreme sadness and loss and it seemed to me in those moments as if it wasn't just me but the entire world was weeping and had gone dark with the fresh absence of someone that I

love so I know the feeling of those monastics tearing their hair and weeping and wailing and at the same time in the same moment I felt some appreciation and equanimity and tremendous peace because loss as searing as it can be it's so truthful and so beautiful sad yes and beautiful

and my own tears and my own sadness and anguish are beautiful because they are the consequence of love and this has happened to me every time each fresh grief makes me love the world and other people in all of life more more and more love with more and more grief every single loss I've

experienced every personal and emotional teaching of impermanence that life has been kind enough to offer me has deepened my ability to love I think that people misunderstand the promise that practice offers us practice is not promising us you know bliss joy transcendence all the time it's not

promising us even the absence of difficulty who would want that in a world in which there's so much injustice so much tragedy so much unhappiness illness and death who wants to feel light-hearted and happy and without trouble in a world like that to feel the scourge of

impermanence and loss and to appreciate it at the same time profoundly as the beautiful essence of what it means to be at all this is the deep truth that I hear echoing in Buddha's last words everything vanishes practice continues so we all have to ask ourselves what's important where do

I stake my life and whether we put that question to ourselves you know in that stark way dramatic way or not if you're a human being the question is there and it will be answered it will be answered by your life your life is the answer to that question so I'm so grateful to be able to live my life

in the company of so many of you who are answering that question with courage and real strength knowing what is important and acting on that and when you feel that and when you have confidence in that then you can come when it's time to come and you can go when it's time to go it's

beautiful it's okay so thanks to the community here for I always think you know I mean yes I suffered terribly waiting in the airport for my delayed flight always me was just awful meantime everybody here is like working and madly to put on this retreat you know cooking the food and shopping

this that and the other thing I don't even know all that goes on to make this happen the registrar the people packing all their Zafus into their cars to get there and blah blah all this stuff and I sort of waltz in nice calm he's very calm no wonder I'm calm I don't have to do anything so I'm well

aware of all it takes to make this happen all it takes to bring this hall into our lives and as a gathering place for everybody and the new place in Vancouver anxious to see when I'm up there in May this is a real offering to the world thank you for doing it thank you Tim and everybody in the
community take care
